items.item: S3 Tables launched December 3, 2024 with automatic compaction, snapshot management and unreferenced-file removal; up to 3x faster queries and 10x higher TPS claimed versus self-managed tables

at.step: Four names, four different things actually automated

sources.source: AWS: Working with Amazon S3 Tables and table buckets

items.item: A table bucket is a storage type purpose-built for Iceberg tables, distinct from a general-purpose bucket

sources.source: AWS: Working with Apache Iceberg V3

items.item: Amazon Athena cannot read Iceberg V3 tables; AWS's own guidance calls the V2-to-V3 upgrade one-way and tells operators to verify every engine's support before upgrading

at.step: AWS's own engine can't read its own newer format

items.item: BigQuery's managed Iceberg tables automate compaction, clustering, and garbage collection past the time-travel window — a different automation set than AWS's

items.item: Unity Catalog manages all read/write/storage/optimization responsibilities, and its Iceberg REST Catalog grants external Iceberg clients read, write and create access

items.item: Snowflake performs maintenance automatically only on Snowflake-managed Iceberg tables; the customer's own engine must maintain externally managed ones

items.item: The hook's point is that 'managed' doesn't mean 'immune to every failure mode'; a learner who concludes a managed service removes all operational risk has drawn the wrong lesson from topic 3 being solved

at.step: A managed service that was supposed to make this mistake impossible

items.item: The predict step's correct answer is structural, not a vendor's mistake: the writer and the reader are simply two independently-versioned pieces of software, and nothing requires them to upgrade in lockstep

items.item: The four vendor cards are deliberately not reduced to a single checklist; a learner who comes away thinking 'they all do the same three things' has missed the entire teaching point of this topic, unlike topic 8's five-names-one-mechanism framing

at.step: Four names, four different things actually automated

items.item: The per-request premium is additive to, not a replacement for, topic 6's four-dimension cost model — storage and requests are still billed normally underneath the monitoring and compaction fees

at.step: The bill for not doing it yourself

items.item: 'Maintenance as a service' is a timing-and-control trade, not a strictly cheaper-or-more-expensive one; a learner should be able to state which variable (cost or control) they're giving up before picking a side

at.step: Someone still owns the job, just a different someone

items.item: Using Amazon Athena's own documented V3 gap as the example (rather than a generic unnamed engine) matters pedagogically: it proves this is a real, current, named constraint and not an invented worst case

items.item: The worked reproduction's power is holding the table, the data and the files constant and varying only the metadata's format-version field — a learner who thinks the data itself needs to change for an engine to break has misunderstood the mechanism

items.item: The recap's three lines are not independent trivia; a learner who can name all four vendors but can't say why a one-way spec upgrade is risky has learned the vocabulary, not the lesson

items.item: The prove-it question generalizes past this topic: 'pin and freeze' is never a permanent fix for a moving external dependency, which is the same lesson as any vendor-controlled default that changes on its own schedule
